items.readable_text:
Content:
To calculate the line integral of a function [MATH: f(x,y)] along a curve [MATH: C,] we use the formula

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.]

Content:
The curve [MATH: C] must be parametrized by the vector function [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] to apply this formula.

Content:
Now suppose we want to evaluate the line integral

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle \int \limits_{C} \dfrac{y}{x} \,\textrm ds,]
where [MATH: C] is the section of the curve [MATH: y = x^2] between the points [MATH: (0,0)] and [MATH: (1,1).]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/64c817ee9579fb95f93ba7a9e86bcb86]

Content:
To reduce the calculation of the line integral to a parametric case, we must first parametrize the curve.

Content:
Notice that the curve [MATH: C] is of the form [MATH: y = y(x).] Therefore, by setting [MATH: x=t,] we have [MATH: y = y(t) = t^2.] This gives the following parametrization for [MATH: C\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle t, t^2 \right\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \le 1.]

Content:
Computing [MATH: \| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,] we get

Content:
[MATH: ‖r^{′}(t)‖|= sqrt((x^{′}(t))^{2} + (y^{′}(t))^{2}); = sqrt(1^{2} + (2t)^{2}); = sqrt(1 + 4t^{2}).]

Content:
Also, using [MATH: x=t] and [MATH: y=t^2,] we have

Content:
[MATH: f(r(t)) = (y)/(x) = (t^{2})/(t) = t.]

Content:
Therefore, we can express the line integral in terms of [MATH: t] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: ∫_(C)(y)/(x)ds|= ∫_{a}^{b}f(r(t))‖r^{′}(t)‖dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}tsqrt(1 + 4t^{2})dt]

sections.normalized_html: Consider the line integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int \limits_{C} \dfrac{y^2}{x} \,\textrm ds,] where [MATH: C] is the section of the curve [MATH: y = \dfrac{x^3}3] between the points [MATH: (0,0)] and [MATH: (3,9).] Write the line integral in the form [MATH: \displaystyle\int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.]

Consider the line integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int \limits_{C} \dfrac{y^2}{x} \,\textrm ds,] where [MATH: C] is the section of the curve [MATH: y = \dfrac{x^3}3] between the points [MATH: (0,0)] and [MATH: (3,9).]
Write the line integral in the form [MATH: \displaystyle\int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that the given curve is of the form [MATH: y=y(x).] Therefore, by setting [MATH: x=t,] we have [MATH: y = y(t) = \dfrac{t^3}{3}.] This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

[MATH: \mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle t, \dfrac{t^3}3 \right\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \le 3,]

Computing [MATH: \mathbf{r}'(t)] and [MATH: \| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,] we get the following:

[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j; = (d)/(dt)(t)i + (d)/(dt)((t^{3})/(3))j; = i + t^{2}j; ‖r^{′}(t)‖|= sqrt(((dx)/(dt))^{2} + ((dy)/(dt))^{2}); = sqrt(1^{2} + (t^{2})^{2}); = sqrt(1 + t^{4})]

Now, since [MATH: f(x,y) = \dfrac{y^2}{x},] we obtain

[MATH: f(r(t))|= (((t^{3})/(3))^{2})/(t) = (1)/(9)t^{5}.]

Therefore, we can write the integral as

[MATH: ∫_(C)f(x, y)ds|= ∫_{0}^{3}f(r(t))‖r^{′}(t)‖dt; = ∫_{0}^{3}(1)/(9)t^{5} ⋅ sqrt(1 + t^{4}) ⋅ dt; = (1)/(9)∫_{0}^{3}t^{5}sqrt(1 + t^{4})dt.]

Item 5 — Example: Computing a Line Integral of a Scalar Function Along a Curve Given in Explicit Cartesian Form

Example Prompt:
Evaluate the integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \dfrac{y^3}{x^2} \, \text{d}s,] where the curve [MATH: C] is given by [MATH: y = x] for [MATH: \, 0 \le x \le 4.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Notice that the given curve is of the form [MATH: y=y(x).] Therefore, by setting [MATH: x=t,] we have [MATH: y = y(t) = t.] This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

[MATH: \mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle t, \: t \right\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \le 4]

Computing [MATH: \mathbf{r}'(t)] and [MATH: \| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,] we get the following:

[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j; = (d)/(dt)(t)i + (d)/(dt)(t)j; = i + j; ‖r^{′}(t)‖|= sqrt(((dx)/(dt))^{2} + ((dy)/(dt))^{2}); = sqrt(1^{2} + 1^{2}); = sqrt(2)]

Now, since [MATH: f(x,y) = \dfrac{y^3}{x^2}], we obtain
[MATH: f(r(t))|= (t^{3})/(t^{2}) = t.]

Therefore, we can write the integral as

[MATH: ∫_(C)(y^{3})/(x^{2})ds|= ∫_{0}^{4}f(r(t))‖r^{′}(t)‖dt; = ∫_{0}^{4}t ⋅ sqrt(2) ⋅ dt; = sqrt(2)∫_{0}^{4}tdt; = (sqrt(2))/(2)t^{2}|_{0}^{4}; = (sqrt(2))/(2)(4^{2} − 0^{2}); = 8sqrt(2).]
